phy_ocra.2.0.summary: A gas is made of particles moving randomly at high speed in all directions. Their collisions with the walls of the container exert a force, and the force per unit area is the **gas pressure**. The **temperature** of a gas is related to the **average kinetic energy** of its particles, so heating a gas in a sealed, fixed-volume container makes the particles move faster, hit the walls more often and harder, and the pressure **increases**. OCR requires this relationship qualitatively, explained in terms of particle motion.

core.p: The particle model describes a gas as a large number of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) that are **far apart** compared with their size and move **randomly** at high speed in **all directions**.
bullets: Particles move in **straight lines** between collisions.
They collide with **each other** and with the **walls** of the container.
Forces between gas particles are **very weak** (negligible) except during collisions.
Particles have a **range of speeds**; some are fast and some are slow.
Most of a gas is **empty space**, which is why gases can be compressed.

callouts.p: Gas particles are in constant random motion in all directions. This motion causes gas pressure.

core.p: **Pressure** is the force acting **at right angles (normal)** to a surface per unit area. Gas pressure is caused by the force of particles colliding with a surface.
bullets: pressure = force / area, measured in **pascals (Pa)**, where 1 Pa = 1 N/m2.
Gas pressure acts **equally in all directions** on the walls of a container.
More force on the same area means **greater pressure**.
Pressure from a gas acts on **any** surface the gas touches, inside or outside the container.

callouts.p: The total force exerted by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container, per unit area, acting at right angles to the walls.

core.p: When a particle hits a wall and bounces back, its direction of motion reverses. Changing a particle's motion needs a force, so the wall pushes on the particle and (by Newton's third law) the particle pushes on the wall.
bullets: Each collision produces a tiny **force on the wall**.
Billions of collisions every second add up to a steady **overall force**.
The force acts **at right angles** to the wall.
Pressure depends on: **how often** particles hit the walls (collision frequency) and **how hard** they hit (the force of each collision).
Higher speed means each collision has a **bigger change in momentum**, so a bigger force.

callouts.p: For full marks, always mention both: particles collide more frequently AND with more force.

core.p: The **temperature** of a gas is related to the **average kinetic energy** of its particles. The hotter the gas, the faster its particles move on average.
bullets: Heating a gas transfers energy to the **kinetic energy store** of its particles.
Higher temperature means **higher average speed** of the particles.
Lower temperature means particles move **more slowly** on average.
Not all particles have the same speed; temperature relates to the **average**.
Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so a small rise in speed is a bigger rise in kinetic energy.

callouts.p: Increasing the temperature of a gas increases the average kinetic energy (and average speed) of its particles.

core.h: Pressure and temperature at constant volume
core.p: If a gas is kept in a sealed container of **fixed volume** and heated, its **pressure increases**. If it is cooled, its pressure decreases. The volume and mass (number of particles) stay the same.
bullets: Temperature rises, so particles gain kinetic energy and move **faster**.
Faster particles hit the walls **more frequently** (they cross the container more quickly).
Each collision is **harder**, with a greater change of momentum, so a **greater force**.
Greater total force on the same area of wall means **greater pressure**.
The relationship is: as temperature **increases**, pressure **increases** (at constant volume).
Cooling does the reverse: slower particles, fewer and weaker collisions, lower pressure.

callouts.p: Particles gain kinetic energy / move faster; collide with walls more often and with more force; so greater force per unit area, so pressure increases.

core.h: The graph of pressure against temperature
core.p: For a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, a graph of pressure against temperature shows pressure **increasing** as temperature increases. OCR assesses this **qualitatively**: you need to describe and explain the trend, not use a formula.
bullets: The line slopes **upwards**: higher temperature, higher pressure.
Over the range measured in the lab, the line is approximately **straight**.
Volume and the mass of gas must be **kept constant** for this trend.
If the container leaked (mass decreased), the pressure would be lower at each temperature.

callouts.p: Pressure is not directly proportional to temperature in degrees Celsius: the line does not pass through 0 C. Just say pressure increases as temperature increases.

core.h: Why the volume must be constant
core.p: If the volume could change, a heated gas would **expand** instead, and the pressure might not rise. This point is only about a **sealed, rigid** container.
bullets: Fixed volume means particles have the **same distance** to travel between walls.
The only change is the **speed** of the particles, caused by the temperature change.
Keeping mass constant means the **number of particles** stays the same.
Changing volume at constant temperature is a separate idea (pressure and volume, triple content).

core.p: Heating a gas increases its **internal energy**. In a gas the particles are far apart with negligible forces, so almost all of this goes into the **kinetic energy** of the particles, which raises the temperature.
bullets: Energy is transferred by heating from a hotter object to the gas.
Kinetic energy store of the particles increases.
Temperature increases, so pressure increases at constant volume.
Energy is **conserved**; the gas does no work if its volume does not change.

core.p: Many exam questions set the idea in a real context. Apply the same particle chain each time.
bullets: **Car tyres**: after a long drive the tyre air is hotter, so the tyre pressure is higher. Check pressure when tyres are cold.
**Aerosol cans** carry 'do not heat' warnings: heating increases pressure and the can may **explode**.
**Footballs** feel softer on a cold day because the air pressure inside is lower.
**Pressure cookers** and sealed jars: heating raises pressure inside.
A **sealed bottle** taken from a warm room into a freezer may be crushed slightly, because the pressure inside falls below the outside pressure.

callouts.p: Name the change (temperature rises), the particle effect (faster, more frequent, harder collisions), and the result (pressure rises, so the risk).

core.p: The relationship can be shown with a sealed flask of air connected to a **pressure gauge**, heated in a water bath.
bullets: A fixed mass of air is sealed in a rigid flask, so volume is constant.
The flask sits in a **water bath**; a thermometer measures the water (and air) temperature.
Heat the water; at regular temperatures, **wait** so the air reaches the water temperature, then read the pressure gauge.
Keep tubing **short** so most of the air is at the measured temperature.
Plot pressure against temperature: pressure rises as temperature rises.

callouts.p: Volume and mass of gas are control variables. Temperature is the independent variable; pressure is the dependent variable.

core.p: Questions may ask about cooling instead of heating. Reverse each step of the chain carefully.
bullets: Temperature decreases, so average kinetic energy decreases.
Particles move **more slowly**.
They collide with the walls **less often** and with **less force**.
Smaller total force per unit area, so **lower pressure**.
If the outside pressure is greater than the inside pressure, there is a **net inward force** and a weak container can be crushed.

analogy.t: Tennis balls on a garage door
analogy.p: Imagine a group of people throwing tennis balls at a garage door from inside a closed garage. The push on the door is like gas pressure. If they throw the balls faster (higher temperature), each ball hits harder and the balls bounce back to them and return to the door more often, so the door is pushed harder overall. Where it breaks down: real gas particles are not thrown by anyone; they move randomly on their own and bounce elastically off each other and the walls, and there are vastly more of them, so the force is smooth rather than a series of separate thuds.

terms.d: The force per unit area exerted at right angles to a surface by gas particles colliding with it.
Force acting normal to a surface divided by the area of that surface; unit pascal (Pa).
The unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m2.
A measure related to the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance.
Energy stored by a moving object or particle; increases with speed.
Movement in straight lines in all directions, with frequent unpredictable changes caused by collisions.
How often particles hit a surface in a given time.
The gas is kept in a sealed, rigid container so the space it occupies cannot change.
No gas enters or leaves, so the number of particles stays the same.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
Model in which matter is made of tiny particles whose arrangement and motion explain its properties.
A force acting at right angles to a surface.
Instrument that measures the pressure of a gas.

mistakes.w: The particles get bigger when heated so pressure goes up.
mistakes.r: Particles do not change size; they move faster, collide more often and with more force.

mistakes.w: The particles collide with each other more, so pressure increases.
mistakes.r: Pressure comes from collisions with the walls of the container.

mistakes.w: There are more particles when the gas is heated.
mistakes.r: The number of particles (mass) is fixed; only their speed changes.

mistakes.w: Only says 'more collisions'.
mistakes.r: Say more frequent collisions with the walls AND each collision exerts a greater force.

mistakes.w: Pressure is directly proportional to temperature in C.
mistakes.r: Pressure increases as temperature increases at constant volume (qualitative); it is not proportional to Celsius temperature.

mistakes.w: The particles vibrate faster.
mistakes.r: Gas particles move randomly and freely; say they move faster (greater average speed/kinetic energy).

mistakes.w: Heating the gas makes it expand so pressure rises.
mistakes.r: At constant volume the gas cannot expand; pressure rises because particles move faster.

mistakes.w: Temperature is the energy of the gas.
mistakes.r: Temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles.

exam.q: State what is meant by the pressure of a gas.
model: Force per unit area exerted by gas particles colliding with the surface (at right angles)
exam.tip: Mention force and area.

exam.q: Explain how gas particles exert a pressure on the walls of a container.
model: Particles collide with the walls / change direction (momentum)
Each collision exerts a force on the wall; total force per unit area is pressure
exam.tip: Collisions with walls, not each other.

exam.q: State what happens to the average speed of gas particles when the temperature increases.
model: It increases
exam.tip: Short answer, no explanation needed.

exam.q: A sealed rigid container of gas is heated. State what happens to the pressure.
model: Pressure increases
exam.tip: Rigid means constant volume.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure of a gas in a sealed container increases when it is heated.
model: Particles gain kinetic energy / move faster
They collide with the walls more frequently
Each collision exerts a greater force (greater change in momentum)
So greater force per unit area, so pressure increases
exam.tip: Four distinct steps for four marks.

exam.q: Explain why aerosol cans carry the warning 'do not expose to high temperatures'.
model: Higher temperature means particles move faster
More frequent and harder collisions with the can walls, so pressure increases
The can could burst / explode
exam.tip: Finish with the consequence.

exam.q: Car tyre pressures should be checked when the tyres are cold. Explain why.
model: After driving the air in the tyres is warmer
Particles move faster so pressure is higher
So the reading would not be the correct (cold) pressure
exam.tip: Link context to particle motion.

exam.q: A football is left outside on a cold night and feels soft in the morning. Explain why.
model: Air inside cools, particles lose kinetic energy / move slower
Fewer collisions per second and less force per collision with the inside walls
So pressure inside decreases
exam.tip: Reverse the heating chain.

exam.q: Describe how the pressure of a gas changes with temperature at constant volume, and explain this using the particle model.
model: As temperature increases, pressure increases (and decreases when cooled)
Volume and mass are fixed, so same number of particles in the same space
Temperature is related to average kinetic energy of particles
Higher temperature means particles move faster
So they collide with walls more often and with greater force
Greater total force on the same area so greater pressure
exam.tip: Describe the trend first, then a full logical explanation.

exam.q: A student heats a sealed flask of air in a water bath and records the pressure. Name the independent, dependent and one control variable.
model: Independent: temperature
Dependent: pressure
Control: volume (or mass of gas)
exam.tip: Volume is the key control variable.

worked.q: Model answer: A sealed glass jar of air is put in hot water. Explain what happens to the pressure inside.
steps: The air inside is heated, so its temperature increases.
The air particles gain kinetic energy and move faster on average.
They hit the inside walls of the jar more frequently.
Each collision exerts a larger force because the particles are moving faster.
The volume is fixed, so the same area receives a larger total force.
worked.ans: The pressure inside the jar increases.

worked.q: Applied example: a student records pressure readings of 100 kPa at 20 C, 107 kPa at 40 C and 114 kPa at 60 C for a sealed flask. Describe the pattern and predict the pressure at 80 C.
steps: Each 20 C rise gives a 7 kPa rise, so the pattern is steady (straight line).
The line does not go through 0 kPa at 0 C, so pressure is not proportional to Celsius temperature.

worked.q: Using pressure = force / area: gas in a container exerts a total force of 500 N on a wall of area 0.025 m2. Calculate the pressure. Then state what happens to the force on the wall if the gas is heated at constant volume.
steps: Heating makes particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent and harder.
worked.ans: 20 000 Pa; the force on the wall increases, so the pressure increases

phy_ocra.2.1.summary: Gases can be **compressed** or **expanded** by changing the pressure on them, and the pressure of a gas produces a **net force at right angles** to any surface it touches. For a **fixed mass of gas at constant temperature**, squashing it into a smaller volume makes the particles hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises; letting it expand lowers the pressure. This is summed up by **pressure x volume = constant**, so p1 x V1 = p2 x V2, which you must be able to apply in calculations and explain with the particle model.

core.h: Gases can be compressed and expanded
core.p: In a gas the particles are **far apart** with lots of empty space between them, so a gas can be squashed into a smaller volume (**compressed**) or allowed to spread into a larger volume (**expanded**). This happens when the pressure on the gas changes.
bullets: Increasing the pressure on a gas **compresses** it (volume decreases).
Decreasing the pressure on a gas lets it **expand** (volume increases).
Solids and liquids are almost **incompressible** because their particles are already touching.
A gas always **fills its container**, spreading out to occupy the whole volume.
Examples: pumping up a tyre, a bicycle pump, a syringe with the end blocked, a weather balloon expanding as it rises.

callouts.p: Gas particles are widely spaced, so pressure can push them closer together; the particles themselves do not get smaller.

core.h: Pressure acts at right angles to surfaces
core.p: The pressure of a gas produces a **net force at right angles (normal)** to any surface, including the walls of its container. This is because particles hit the surface from many directions, and the sideways parts of their pushes cancel out, leaving a push straight into the surface.
bullets: Force from gas pressure = pressure x area, acting **perpendicular** to the surface.
It acts on **every** surface in contact with the gas, in all directions.
A balloon is round because the gas pushes outwards equally at right angles to its surface everywhere.
If the pressure is different on two sides of a surface, there is a **net (resultant) force** towards the lower-pressure side.

callouts.p: The pressure of a gas produces a net force at right angles to the walls of the container (or any surface).

fig.cap: Gas pressure inside a balloon pushes outwards at right angles to the surface at every point, which is why an inflated balloon takes a rounded shape.

core.h: Compressing at constant temperature: particle explanation
core.p: If a fixed mass of gas is compressed into a smaller volume **at constant temperature**, its pressure **increases**. The particles still have the same average speed (same temperature), but they are packed into a smaller space.
bullets: Temperature is constant, so the **average kinetic energy and speed** of the particles do not change.
So each collision with the wall has the **same force** as before.
The particles are **closer together** and have less distance to travel between walls.
So they hit each unit area of wall **more frequently**.
More collisions per second per unit area means a greater force per unit area, so **greater pressure**.

callouts.p: When compressing at constant temperature, only the collision FREQUENCY increases, not the force of each collision. Do not say particles move faster.

core.p: If a fixed mass of gas is allowed to expand into a larger volume at constant temperature, its pressure **decreases**.
bullets: Average speed of particles stays the **same** (temperature constant).
Particles are **further apart** and travel further between collisions with the walls.
They hit each unit area of the walls **less frequently**.
Smaller force per unit area, so **lower pressure**.
Example: a balloon released into the upper atmosphere expands as outside pressure falls.

core.h: The relationship: pressure x volume = constant
core.p: For a **fixed mass of gas at constant temperature**, pressure is **inversely proportional** to volume. If the volume halves, the pressure doubles. OCR states this as **pressure x volume = constant**.
bullets: **p x V = constant**
p = pressure in **pascals (Pa)**
V = volume in **m3** (any volume unit works if both volumes use the same unit)
For a change from state 1 to state 2: **p1 x V1 = p2 x V2**
Only true if the **temperature and the mass of gas** stay constant.
Doubling the pressure halves the volume; tripling the volume makes the pressure one third.

callouts.p: Pressure x volume = constant, for a given mass of gas at constant temperature. Learn it and apply it.
Always state 'fixed mass' and 'constant temperature' when quoting the relationship.

core.p: Because p and V are inversely proportional, a graph of pressure against volume is a **curve** that gets closer to the axes but never touches them. A graph of pressure against **1 / volume** is a **straight line through the origin**.
bullets: p against V: a downward **curve** (inverse proportion).
At any point on the curve, p x V gives the **same value**.
p against 1/V: **straight line through the origin**, which proves p is inversely proportional to V.
A gas at a **higher** constant temperature gives a curve **further** from the axes (larger p V).

callouts.p: Show p x V is the same for every pair of readings, or plot p against 1/V and show a straight line through the origin.

core.p: Most calculations give you a starting pressure and volume, then one new value, and ask for the other.
bullets: Write down p1, V1, p2, V2 and identify the **unknown**.
Rearrange: **V2 = p1 V1 / p2** or **p2 = p1 V1 / V2**.
Check the answer makes sense: smaller volume should give **bigger** pressure.
Volumes can be in cm3 on both sides, and pressures in kPa on both sides, as long as units match.
Give the unit for the answer.

callouts.p: If the volume goes down, your pressure must go up. If not, you have rearranged wrongly.

core.p: Compressing a gas quickly does **work** on it and can raise its temperature (a separate spec point). For p V = constant to hold, the gas must be compressed **slowly** so it stays at the same temperature as its surroundings.
bullets: If the temperature rises, particles move faster and pressure rises **more** than predicted.
In experiments, change the volume **slowly** and wait before taking readings.
A fixed mass is needed: a leaking seal would change the number of particles.

core.p: The relationship can be investigated with a sealed syringe or a column of trapped air connected to a **pressure gauge**.
bullets: Trap a fixed mass of air in a syringe or tube; seal it so no air escapes.
Change the pressure (push the piston or use a pump) and record pressure from the **gauge** and volume from the **scale**.
Wait after each change so the air returns to **room temperature**.
Repeat for a range of values; calculate p x V for each pair.
Plot p against V (curve) and p against 1/V (straight line through origin).
Read the volume at **eye level** to avoid parallax error.

core.p: If the gas pressure on one side of a surface is bigger than on the other, there is a **resultant force** on the surface towards the lower pressure. This explains many effects of compressing or expanding gases.
bullets: Net force = pressure difference x area.
A sealed crisp packet taken up a mountain **puffs up** because outside pressure falls, so the gas inside expands.
Pumping air into a tyre increases the inside pressure, giving an outward force that keeps it firm.
A syringe plunger with a blocked end becomes harder to push in, because the trapped gas pressure increases.

callouts.p: Things are pushed by the higher pressure, not pulled by a vacuum. Describe the net force from the pressure difference.

core.p: Everyday technology depends on compressing and expanding gases.
bullets: **Bicycle pumps** compress air to a higher pressure to push it into the tyre.
**Scuba tanks** store large amounts of air compressed into a small volume at high pressure.
**Air bubbles** rising in water get bigger because the pressure on them falls.
**Aerosols** and spray cans release compressed gas, which expands as it leaves.

analogy.p: Imagine the same number of people walking at the same speed in a corridor. Make the corridor shorter (smaller volume) and each person reaches the end walls more often, so the walls get bumped more times per second (higher pressure), even though nobody walks faster or bumps harder. Where it breaks down: real gas particles move randomly in three dimensions at very high speeds, bounce elastically, and the pressure change is exactly inversely proportional to volume, which a corridor of people would not show.

terms.d: Decreasing the volume of a gas by increasing the pressure on it.
Increase in the volume of a gas when the pressure on it decreases.
Force per unit area exerted by gas particles colliding with a surface, producing a net force at right angles to it.
Unit of pressure, equal to 1 N/m2.
When one quantity doubles the other halves; their product is constant.
For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure multiplied by volume does not change.
No gas enters or leaves, so the number of particles is constant.
Temperature does not change, so the average kinetic energy of particles is constant.
Number of particle collisions with a unit area of wall per second.
Force acting at right angles to a surface.
Overall force when all forces on an object are combined; from pressure differences it acts towards lower pressure.
Instrument used to measure the pressure of a gas.
Space occupied by the gas, measured in m3 (or cm3).

mistakes.w: When compressed, the particles move faster so pressure increases.
mistakes.r: At constant temperature speed is unchanged; particles hit the walls more frequently because they are closer together.

mistakes.w: The particles get squashed / smaller.
mistakes.r: The particles stay the same size; the spaces between them decrease.

mistakes.w: Pressure is directly proportional to volume.
mistakes.r: Pressure is inversely proportional to volume: p x V = constant.
p1 x V1 = p2 x V2.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the conditions.
mistakes.r: State fixed mass of gas and constant temperature.

mistakes.w: Gas pressure acts only downwards.
mistakes.r: Gas pressure produces a force at right angles to every surface, in all directions.

mistakes.w: A p against V graph is a straight line with negative gradient.
mistakes.r: It is a curve; p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin.

mistakes.w: Mixing units, e.g. cm3 on one side and m3 on the other.
mistakes.r: Use the same units for both volumes and both pressures.

model: Pressure increases

model: At right angles (perpendicular / normal) to the walls
exam.tip: Use 'right angles'.

exam.q: Explain why gases can be compressed but liquids cannot be compressed easily.

Liquid particles are touching so cannot be pushed closer together

exam.q: A gas has a pressure of 100 kPa and volume 60 cm3. It is compressed at constant temperature to 20 cm3. Calculate the new pressure.
model: p1 V1 = p2 V2
p2 = 300 kPa
exam.tip: Units can stay as kPa and cm3 if consistent.

exam.q: Explain, using the particle model, why compressing a gas at constant temperature increases its pressure.
model: Same number of particles in a smaller volume
Temperature constant so particles have the same average speed / kinetic energy
Particles collide with the walls more frequently
Greater force per unit area so greater pressure
exam.tip: Do not say particles move faster.

exam.q: A diver releases an air bubble of volume 2.0 cm3 at a depth where the pressure is 300 kPa. Calculate its volume at the surface where pressure is 100 kPa. Assume the temperature is constant.
model: p1 V1 = p2 V2
exam.tip: Lower pressure, so the volume should be bigger.

exam.q: A sealed crisp packet puffs up when taken to the top of a mountain. Explain why.
model: Atmospheric pressure outside is lower at altitude
Pressure inside is greater than outside, giving a net outward force
So the gas inside expands until pressures balance
exam.tip: Mention the pressure difference.

exam.q: Describe an experiment to investigate how the pressure of a gas depends on its volume, and explain how the results show the relationship.
model: Trap a fixed mass of air in a sealed syringe/tube connected to a pressure gauge
Change the volume (or pressure) in steps and record pressure and volume
Change slowly and wait so temperature stays constant
Read volume at eye level; repeat readings
Calculate p x V for each pair: it is constant
Or plot p against 1/V: a straight line through the origin shows p inversely proportional to V
exam.tip: Include method, control of temperature, and analysis.

exam.q: Gas at 200 kPa occupies 0.030 m3. At constant temperature its pressure is reduced to 50 kPa. Calculate the new volume.
model: V2 = p1 V1 / p2
exam.tip: Pressure divided by 4 so volume x 4.

exam.q: State two conditions needed for pressure x volume to remain constant.
model: Fixed / constant mass of gas
Constant temperature
exam.tip: Both needed.

steps: Sense check: volume reduced to one third, pressure tripled.

A student's readings are: 100 kPa at 30 cm3, 150 kPa at 20 cm3, 200 kPa at 15 cm3. Show that the results obey p x V = constant.

phy_ocra.2.2.summary: **Doing work on a gas** means using a force to compress it, for example pushing the piston of a bicycle pump. Work done is energy transferred, so this energy goes into the **internal energy** of the gas, increasing the **kinetic energy** of its particles and so its **temperature**. This is why a bicycle pump gets warm when you pump up a tyre quickly. The reverse also happens: when a gas expands and does work on its surroundings, it loses energy and cools.

core.h: What 'doing work on a gas' means
core.p: **Work is done** when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force. When you push a piston into a cylinder of gas, you apply a force over a distance, so you **do work on the gas**.
bullets: **work done (J) = force (N) x distance (m)**, in the direction of the force.
Work done is the same as **energy transferred** (1 J of work = 1 J of energy).
Compressing a gas requires a force against the gas pressure, so **work must be done**.
The energy transferred goes into the gas's **internal energy** store.

callouts.p: Energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance: work done = force x distance (along the line of action of the force).

core.h: Doing work on a gas increases its temperature
core.p: When work is done on a gas by compressing it quickly, energy is transferred to the gas. This increases the **internal energy** of the gas, and in a gas this mostly means increasing the **kinetic energy** of the particles, so the **temperature rises**.
bullets: Mechanical work by a force becomes energy in the gas's **internal (thermal) energy store**.
Particles gain **kinetic energy**, so they move faster on average.
Higher average kinetic energy means a **higher temperature**.
The faster the compression, the less time for energy to escape to the surroundings, so the **bigger the temperature rise**.

callouts.p: Doing work on a gas increases its internal energy and can increase its temperature.

core.p: At particle level, the piston moving inwards acts like a bat hitting a ball. Particles that bounce off the **moving** piston rebound **faster** than they hit it, so they gain kinetic energy.
bullets: Gas particles collide with the inward-moving piston.
The piston **pushes** on each particle as it collides, doing work on it.
Each particle **rebounds with a higher speed** than it arrived with.
Across billions of collisions, the **average kinetic energy** of the particles increases.
So the **temperature** of the gas increases.

callouts.p: The temperature rise is caused by particles bouncing off a piston that is moving towards them, not simply by the particles being closer together.

fig.cap: A particle collides with a piston moving inwards. It rebounds with a higher speed than before (longer arrow), so it has gained kinetic energy from the work done by the piston.

core.p: The classic example is a **bicycle pump**. When you pump up a tyre quickly, the barrel of the pump gets noticeably **warm**, especially near the outlet end.
bullets: Each push of the handle does **work** on the air inside the pump.
Air is **compressed**, and its internal energy and temperature increase.
Energy is transferred by heating from the hot air to the **barrel** of the pump.
The end nearest the valve gets **hottest**, where the air is most compressed.
Friction between the piston and barrel also adds a little heating, but the **main** cause is work done on the gas.

callouts.p: Do not say the pump gets hot only because of friction. The main cause is work done compressing the air.

core.p: **Internal energy** is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a system. In a gas, the forces between particles are very small, so increasing internal energy mostly increases the **kinetic energy** of the particles.
bullets: Temperature is related to the **average kinetic energy** of the particles.
Work done on the gas increases its internal energy.
So the temperature rises (unless the energy is transferred away fast enough).
Energy is **conserved**: work done = increase in internal energy + energy transferred to surroundings.

core.p: Whether the temperature rises depends on how quickly the gas is compressed compared with how quickly energy can escape.
bullets: **Fast compression**: little time for energy to be transferred to the surroundings, so the gas gets **hot**.
**Slow compression**: energy has time to escape through the walls, so the gas stays at about **constant temperature**.
This is why p x V = constant only applies to **slow** compression at constant temperature.
Fast compression gives a **greater pressure rise** than p V = constant predicts, because the temperature also rises.

callouts.p: If a question mixes compression and temperature, decide first whether the compression is quick (temperature rises) or slow (temperature constant).

core.h: The reverse: a gas doing work cools
core.p: When a gas **expands**, it pushes a piston or the surroundings outwards, so the **gas does work** on its surroundings. Energy is transferred out of the gas, so its internal energy and temperature **decrease**.
bullets: Particles bounce off a piston moving **away** from them and rebound **slower**.
Average kinetic energy falls, so temperature falls.
Example: gas released quickly from an aerosol can or a CO2 cartridge makes the nozzle feel **cold**.
Example: a tyre valve feels cool when air rushes out.

callouts.p: Work done ON a gas: temperature rises. Work done BY a gas (expanding): temperature falls.

core.p: You can calculate the work done on a gas using **work done = force x distance**. All of this energy is transferred to the gas (minus any energy lost).
bullets: Force in **newtons (N)**, distance in **metres (m)**, work in **joules (J)**.
Convert cm to m by dividing by 100.
Work done on the gas over several strokes = work per stroke x number of strokes.
If no energy were lost, increase in internal energy = work done.

callouts.p: A pump stroke of 30 cm is 0.30 m. Using cm gives an answer 100 times too big.

core.p: Doing work on a gas appears in several real-life contexts.
bullets: **Diesel engines**: air is compressed so quickly in the cylinder that it becomes hot enough to **ignite the fuel** without a spark.
**Fire syringe (fire piston)**: rapidly pushing a piston into a sealed tube heats the air enough to ignite cotton wool.
**Compressors** (e.g. in refrigerators and air tools) get hot as they compress gas.
**Pumping up a football** quickly warms the pump.

core.p: Many questions ask you to explain why a pump or compressed gas gets hot. A clear chain of reasoning earns all the marks.
bullets: 1. A force moves the piston a distance, so **work is done on the gas**.
2. Energy is transferred to the **internal energy** (kinetic energy store) of the gas particles.
3. Particles rebound from the moving piston **faster**, so average **kinetic energy increases**.
4. So the **temperature of the gas increases**.
5. Energy is then transferred by **heating** to the walls of the container.

analogy.p: A ball bouncing off a wall that is still comes back at the same speed. But if a cricket bat swings towards the ball, the ball flies off much faster: the bat has done work on it. The moving piston is the bat and the gas particles are the balls, so pushing the piston in makes the particles speed up, and the gas gets hotter. Where it breaks down: a gas has billions of particles moving in random directions, most of which never touch the piston in a given moment; the energy is shared out between them by collisions, and temperature depends on their average kinetic energy, not on one particle.

phy_ocra.2.3.summary: The Earth is surrounded by a thin layer of air called the **atmosphere**, held in place by gravity. Air particles move randomly at high speed and collide with every surface, and these collisions produce **atmospheric pressure**, which acts in all directions at right angles to surfaces. Atmospheric pressure is about 100 kPa at sea level and **decreases with height** because there is less air above you, so the weight of air pushing down is smaller and the air is less dense, giving fewer collisions per second.

core.h: A simple model of the atmosphere
core.p: The atmosphere is a relatively **thin layer of gas** around the Earth, kept in place by the Earth's **gravitational pull**. Compared with the radius of the Earth (about 6400 km), most of the air lies within roughly 10 to 15 km of the surface, so the atmosphere is like the skin on an apple.
bullets: Air is a **mixture of gases**: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, plus small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Gravity pulls every air particle **towards the centre of the Earth**, which is why the air does not drift off into space.
The air is **densest at the surface** and becomes **less dense (thinner)** as height increases.
There is no sharp top edge: the air just gets thinner and thinner until it merges into space.
In the particle model, air particles are **far apart** and move **randomly at high speed** in all directions.

callouts.p: A thin layer of gas surrounding the Earth, held in place by gravity, whose density decreases with height.

core.p: Pressure in a gas comes from **particle collisions**. Every time an air particle hits a surface and bounces off, its momentum changes, so it exerts a tiny **force** on the surface. Billions of collisions every second add up to a steady force over each square metre, which is the pressure.
bullets: Air particles **collide with surfaces** (and each other) all the time.
Each collision exerts a small **force at right angles (normal) to the surface**.
The total force per unit area is the **atmospheric pressure**.
More collisions per second, or harder collisions, mean **greater pressure**.
You can also think of it as the **weight of the column of air** above a surface pushing down on it.

callouts.p: The pressure exerted by the atmosphere on a surface, caused by air particles colliding with it; it acts in all directions at right angles to the surface.

Collisions of particles and the weight of the air above are two ways of describing the same pressure. Mark schemes accept both, but explanations of height variation usually need the weight of air above or the density of the air.

core.p: Pressure is defined as **force per unit area**, so the same equation applies to the atmosphere as to anything else. This lets you calculate the huge force the air exerts on everyday objects.
bullets: **pressure = force normal to a surface / area of that surface**, or p = F / A.
Pressure is measured in **pascals (Pa)**; 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
Force in **newtons (N)**, area in **square metres (m²)**.
Rearranged: **F = p × A** and **A = F / p**.
1 kPa = 1000 Pa, so 100 kPa = 100 000 Pa.

callouts.p: Areas are often given in cm². 1 m² = 10 000 cm², so divide cm² by 10 000 to get m² before using p = F / A.

core.p: At sea level, atmospheric pressure is about **100 000 Pa (100 kPa)**; a standard value is about 101 kPa. This means the air pushes on every square metre with a force of about 100 000 N, roughly the weight of a 10 tonne lorry.
bullets: Sea level atmospheric pressure is **about 100 kPa** (about 101 kPa).
It varies slightly with **weather**: high and low pressure systems.
We are not crushed because the pressure **inside our bodies** pushes outwards and **balances** the outside pressure.
A **barometer** measures atmospheric pressure.
Pressure drops noticeably as you climb a mountain or fly in a plane.

callouts.p: Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 100 kPa = 1 × 10^5 Pa.

core.p: Because air particles move **randomly in all directions**, they hit surfaces from every side. That means atmospheric pressure is not just a downward push: it acts **sideways and upwards** too, always at right angles to the surface.
bullets: Random motion means collisions happen **equally from all directions**.
The force from pressure is always **perpendicular (normal) to the surface**.
This is why a sheet of card can hold water in an upturned glass: air pushes **up** on the card.
It is also why a can crushes from all sides when the air inside is removed.

callouts.p: Do not say atmospheric pressure only acts downwards. It acts in all directions at right angles to any surface.

core.h: Why pressure decreases with height: less air above
core.p: As you go **higher**, there is **less air above you**. The column of air above a surface is shorter, so it has **less mass** and therefore **less weight**. A smaller weight pushing on the same area means a **smaller pressure**.
bullets: Higher altitude means a **shorter column of air** above.
Less air above means **smaller weight** of air above.
Smaller force on the same area means **lower pressure** (p = F / A).
At the surface you support the weight of the **whole** atmosphere above you.

callouts.p: Atmospheric pressure decreases with height because there is less air (a smaller weight of air) above the surface.

core.h: Why pressure decreases with height: density
core.p: The air near the ground is **squashed by the weight of the air above it**, so it is **compressed and denser**. Higher up there is less air pressing down, so the air is **less dense**: the particles are **further apart**. Fewer particles per cubic metre means **fewer collisions per second** with a surface, so a lower pressure.
bullets: Density of air **decreases with height**.
Less dense means **fewer particles per unit volume**.
Fewer particles means **fewer collisions per second** with a surface.
Fewer collisions per second means a **smaller force per unit area**, so lower pressure.
Air at higher altitudes is also usually **colder**, so particles move more slowly and hit surfaces less hard.

callouts.p: For full marks link: height increases, so less air above, so air less dense, so fewer collisions per second (smaller weight of air), so lower pressure.

core.h: Shape of the pressure against height graph
core.p: Pressure does **not** fall in a straight line. Because the air near the ground is compressed, most of the mass of the atmosphere is in the lowest few kilometres. Pressure falls **quickly at first** and then **more and more slowly**, curving towards zero.
bullets: The graph is a **curve**, not a straight line.
Steepest near the ground, flattening at greater heights.
Pressure roughly **halves** for every 5 to 6 km of height near the surface.
At the cruising height of an airliner (about 10 km), pressure is only about a quarter of sea level value.
Pressure **never quite reaches zero** within the atmosphere; it approaches zero in space.

callouts.p: A common error is drawing a straight line. The density of air changes with height, so pressure does not decrease by equal amounts for equal height changes.

core.h: Comparing the air at low and high altitude
core.p: A side by side comparison helps you organise the reasoning for longer answers.
bullets: Everything on the right of the table follows from **less air above**.
Breathing is harder at altitude because each breath contains **fewer oxygen molecules**.

core.h: Effects of atmospheric pressure in everyday life
core.p: Atmospheric pressure explains many everyday observations, and exam questions often ask you to apply the idea to a new context.
bullets: **Ears pop** on a plane or in a lift because outside pressure changes while the air trapped in your middle ear is at the old pressure.
A sealed **crisp packet puffs up** on a mountain: inside pressure is higher than the lower outside pressure.
A **suction cup** sticks because air is pushed out; the higher atmospheric pressure outside pushes it onto the surface.
Drinking through a **straw**: you lower the pressure in your mouth and atmospheric pressure pushes the drink up.
Aircraft cabins are **pressurised** because outside pressure at cruising height is too low for comfort and breathing.
A **collapsing can**: when steam inside condenses, inside pressure falls and atmospheric pressure crushes the can.

callouts.p: Things move or deform because of a pressure difference. Always say which side has the higher pressure and which way the resultant force acts.

core.p: The same model applies to any planet with an atmosphere. Atmospheric pressure at the surface depends on **how much gas** is above and the **strength of gravity**.
bullets: More gas above the surface gives a **larger weight** of gas and higher pressure.
A stronger gravitational field strength makes the same gas **weigh more**, increasing pressure.
On every planet, pressure **decreases with height** above the surface for the same reason: less gas above.
A planet with very little atmosphere has a very low surface pressure.

core.p: For **small height changes** the density of air is almost constant, so you can estimate the pressure difference using the same equation used for liquids: pressure difference = height × density × g.
bullets: **p = h × ρ × g**, where h is height difference in m, ρ is density in kg/m³, g is gravitational field strength in N/kg.
Air density near the ground is about **1.2 kg/m³**, much less than water (1000 kg/m³).
So climbing 100 m lowers the pressure by about 100 × 1.2 × 10 = 1200 Pa, about 1% of atmospheric pressure.
For large heights this does **not** work well, because density falls as height increases.

callouts.p: Using p = hρg for the whole atmosphere gives the wrong answer because air density is not constant with height.

analogy.p: Picture a tall pile of soft pillows. The pillow at the bottom carries the weight of all the others, so it is squashed flat and dense; the top pillow carries nothing and is fluffy. If you squeeze your hand into the pile, it is pressed hardest near the bottom and hardly at all near the top. Air behaves the same way: the bottom layers are compressed by the weight above, so pressure and density are greatest at the ground. Where it breaks down: pillows only press downwards, but air pressure acts in all directions, and pressure in air comes from fast moving particles colliding, not from objects resting on each other.

terms.d: Thin layer of gas around the Earth held in place by gravity.
Pressure exerted by the air on a surface due to collisions of air particles; about 100 kPa at sea level.
Force acting normal to a surface divided by the area of that surface (p = F / A).
Unit of pressure equal to one newton per square metre.
A force acting at right angles to a surface.
Mass per unit volume of a substance, measured in kg/m³.
Height above sea level.
Model in which a gas is made of particles that are far apart and move randomly at high speed.
Movement of particles in unpredictable directions with a range of speeds.
When a particle hits a surface or another particle and bounces off, exerting a force.
Force on a mass due to gravity; weight = mass × gravitational field strength.
Force per unit mass due to gravity, about 10 N/kg on Earth.
Instrument that measures atmospheric pressure.
The difference in pressure between two sides of a surface, which causes a resultant force.
1000 pascals.

mistakes.r: Main reason is fewer particles per unit volume, giving fewer collisions per second with a surface.

mistakes.r: It acts in all directions, at right angles to surfaces.

mistakes.w: Pressure falls in a straight line with height.
mistakes.r: Pressure decreases rapidly at first then more slowly, because density decreases with height.

mistakes.w: There is no air pressure in space because there is no gravity.
mistakes.r: There is almost no pressure in space because there are almost no gas particles to collide with surfaces.

mistakes.w: The particles hit the surface more at high altitude because the air is thinner.
mistakes.r: Thinner (less dense) air means fewer collisions per second, so lower pressure.

mistakes.r: Pressure = force normal to a surface divided by area.

mistakes.w: Using area in cm² directly in p = F / A.
mistakes.r: Convert to m² first (divide cm² by 10 000) to get pressure in Pa.

The air becomes less dense (thinner) with increasing height

exam.tip: Rearrange p = F / A before substituting.

Atmospheric pressure outside is lower at higher altitude
Because there is less air above, so the air is less dense
Pressure inside is greater than outside so there is a resultant outward force and the packet expands
exam.tip: Compare inside with outside and state the direction of the resultant force.

exam.q: Sketch and describe how atmospheric pressure changes with height above the surface.
model: Pressure decreases as height increases
Decreases rapidly at first then more slowly (curve, not straight line)
exam.tip: Say the shape in words as well as sketching it.

exam.q: Explain why passengers' ears may pop when a plane climbs.
model: Outside (cabin) pressure decreases as the plane climbs
Air trapped in the ear is at a higher pressure, pushing the eardrum outwards until pressures equalise
exam.tip: Always describe a pressure difference.

exam.q: Explain why we are not crushed by atmospheric pressure.
model: Pressure inside the body (fluids and air) pushes outwards
This balances the atmospheric pressure outside, so there is no resultant force
exam.tip: Use the word balance.

exam.q: Describe and explain how and why atmospheric pressure varies with height above the surface of the Earth. Use ideas about particles in your answer.
model: The atmosphere is a thin layer of air held to the Earth by gravity
Pressure is caused by air particles colliding with surfaces, exerting a force
Atmospheric pressure is about 100 kPa at sea level and decreases with height
At greater height there is less air above, so the weight of the air above is smaller
Lower layers are compressed so air is densest at the surface; higher up there are fewer particles per unit volume
Fewer collisions per second (and colder, slower particles) so smaller force per unit area
Pressure falls quickly near the ground and then more slowly, so the graph is a curve
exam.tip: Level 3 answers give a full logical chain from height to pressure, using particle ideas and the weight of air.

phy_ocra.2.4.summary: Pressure in a liquid is caused by the **weight of the liquid above** a point, so it **increases with depth** and with the **density** of the liquid. Because the bottom of a submerged object is deeper than its top, the pressure (and force) on its bottom is greater, giving a resultant upward force called **upthrust**. The pressure difference is calculated with **p = h × ρ × g**, and whether an object floats or sinks depends on whether upthrust can balance its weight, which comes down to comparing the **density of the object with the density of the liquid**.

core.h: What causes pressure in a liquid
core.p: A liquid has **weight**. At any point in a liquid, the liquid above that point is pulled down by gravity and pushes on the liquid below. The deeper you go, the more liquid there is above, so the **weight of liquid above** and therefore the pressure is greater.
bullets: Pressure in a liquid is due to the **weight of the column of liquid above** a point.
Liquid particles are **close together** and can move past each other, so the liquid transmits the pressure.
Pressure acts **in all directions** at a given depth.
The force from pressure always acts **at right angles (normal) to any surface** in the liquid.
Liquids are almost **incompressible**, so their density is roughly the same at all depths.

callouts.p: Force acting normal to a surface per unit area of that surface: p = F / A, measured in pascals (Pa).

core.p: Double the depth and you double the height of liquid above, so you double its weight on each square metre. So **pressure due to a liquid is directly proportional to depth**.
bullets: Greater depth means **more liquid above**, so greater weight per unit area.
Water squirts **further** from a hole near the bottom of a bottle than from a hole near the top.
Dams are built **thicker at the bottom** because the water pressure is greatest there.
Divers feel greater pressure on their ears the deeper they swim.
Pressure depends on **depth only**, not on the shape or width of the container.

callouts.p: At the same depth in the same liquid, pressure is the same however wide or narrow the container is.

core.p: A **denser** liquid has more mass in each cubic metre, so a column of the same height **weighs more**. This gives a greater pressure at the same depth.
bullets: Greater density means **greater mass per unit volume**.
So the same depth of a denser liquid has a **greater weight above** each square metre.
At the same depth, pressure in sea water (about 1030 kg/m³) is greater than in fresh water (1000 kg/m³).
Pressure also depends on **gravitational field strength g**: on a planet with bigger g, liquid weighs more.

core.h: The equation p = h × ρ × g
core.p: The pressure due to a column of liquid is given by **pressure = height of column × density of liquid × gravitational field strength**. OCR uses it to calculate the **difference in pressure** between two depths.
bullets: **p = h × ρ × g** (Higher tier / triple equation; you must be able to recall and apply it).
h = height of the column (depth) in **metres, m**.
ρ (rho) = density in **kg/m³**.
g = gravitational field strength in **N/kg** (10 N/kg on Earth in OCR papers unless told otherwise; 9.8 is also used).
For a difference: **Δp = Δh × ρ × g**.
Total pressure at depth = **atmospheric pressure + h ρ g**.

callouts.p: Weight of a column = mass × g = (ρ × A × h) × g. Divide by area A to get pressure: p = hρg.
Depth must be in metres and density in kg/m³. Convert cm to m and g/cm³ to kg/m³ (multiply by 1000).

core.p: The surface of a liquid open to the air already has **atmospheric pressure** (about 100 kPa) acting on it. That pressure is transmitted down through the liquid, so the total pressure at a depth is the atmospheric pressure **plus** the pressure due to the liquid.
bullets: Total pressure = **atmospheric pressure + h ρ g**.
In water, pressure increases by about **10 kPa for every 1 m** of depth (1 × 1000 × 10 = 10 000 Pa).
So at about 10 m depth in water the total pressure is roughly **double** atmospheric pressure.
Questions on differences in pressure do not need atmospheric pressure, because it cancels out.

core.p: Consider a block fully submerged in water. Its **bottom surface is deeper** than its top surface, so the water pressure on the bottom is **greater**. Pressure acts at right angles to each surface, so it pushes **down on the top** and **up on the bottom**. Because force = pressure × area and the areas are equal, the upward force is bigger than the downward force. The resultant is an **upward force called upthrust**.
bullets: Pressure on the bottom > pressure on the top because the bottom is **deeper**.
Upward force on the bottom > downward force on the top.
Sideways forces on the vertical faces are **equal and opposite** at each depth, so they cancel.
Resultant force from the liquid = **upthrust, acting upwards**.
Upthrust = pressure difference × area of face = (h ρ g) × A for a simple block.

callouts.p: The resultant upward force exerted by a fluid on a submerged or partly submerged object, caused by the pressure being greater at the bottom of the object than at the top.

callouts.t: Upthrust equals weight of fluid displaced
callouts.p: The upthrust on an object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces (Archimedes' principle). This follows from the pressure difference.

core.p: When an object is put into a liquid it **pushes aside (displaces)** some liquid. The upthrust is exactly equal to the **weight of that displaced liquid**. This gives a quick way to calculate upthrust.
bullets: Upthrust = **weight of fluid displaced** = volume displaced × density of fluid × g.
A fully submerged object displaces its **own volume** of liquid.
A floating object displaces just enough liquid to **equal its own weight**.
Upthrust is greater in a **denser liquid** for the same volume displaced.
Gases exert upthrust too: a helium balloon rises because the upthrust from air exceeds its weight.

core.p: An object floats when the **upthrust equals its weight**. As a floating object is lowered into the liquid it displaces more and more liquid, so upthrust increases. It stops sinking further and floats when upthrust has grown to **balance its weight**.
bullets: Floating: **upthrust = weight**, so the resultant force is zero (in equilibrium).
An object floats if its **average density is less than** the density of the liquid.
Only part of a floating object is under the surface; the denser the object relative to the liquid, the **lower it sits**.
A ship made of steel floats because its hollow shape means its **average density** (steel plus air inside) is less than water.

callouts.p: Floats when weight = upthrust; this is possible when the object's average density is less than (or equal to) the density of the fluid.

core.p: An object sinks when its **weight is greater than the maximum upthrust** it can get. The maximum upthrust happens when the object is fully submerged and displacing its own volume. If that is still less than its weight, there is a **resultant downward force**.
bullets: Sinking: **weight > upthrust** when fully submerged.
Happens when the object's **density is greater than** the density of the liquid.
A solid steel block sinks, but the same mass of steel shaped into a hull can float.
A submarine sinks by taking water into ballast tanks, increasing its **average density**.

callouts.p: It is density, not mass or weight alone, that decides. A huge log floats while a small stone sinks.

core.p: The spec asks you to describe the factors that influence floating and sinking. They all come back to comparing weight and upthrust, which is the same as comparing densities.
bullets: **Density of the object** (its average density, including any air inside).
**Density of the liquid**: denser liquids give more upthrust, so objects float higher in sea water than fresh water.
**Volume of liquid displaced**, which depends on the object's **shape and volume**.
**Weight of the object**, which depends on its mass (and g).
A person floats more easily in the Dead Sea because the very salty water is much **denser**.

core.p: Exam questions often set these ideas in real contexts. Use the language of pressure differences, upthrust and density.
bullets: **Ships** carry a load line (Plimsoll line) because they float at different depths in water of different density and temperature.
**Submarines** control depth by changing average density with ballast tanks.
**Hot air balloons** rise because hot air is less dense than the surrounding air.
**Dam walls** are thicker at the base to withstand the greater pressure.
**Hydrometers** float lower in less dense liquids, so they can measure density.

callouts.p: Pressure increases with depth, so bottom pressure > top pressure, so upward force > downward force, so upthrust; then compare upthrust with weight to decide float or sink.

analogy.t: A stack of people in a crowd
analogy.p: Imagine people lying on top of each other in a pile. The person at the bottom feels the weight of everyone above, so the deeper in the pile, the bigger the squash: that is pressure increasing with depth. Heavier people (denser liquid) make the squash bigger for the same number of layers. If you slide a box into the pile, the people below push up on its base harder than the people above push down on its lid, so the box is pushed upwards: that is upthrust. Where it breaks down: a pile of people only pushes up and down, but liquid pressure pushes equally in all directions, including sideways.

1 Pa = 1 N/m².
Mass per unit volume, ρ = m / V, in kg/m³.
Vertical distance below the surface of a liquid.
The liquid directly above a point, whose weight causes pressure at that point.
Force per unit mass due to gravity, g, about 10 N/kg on Earth.
Resultant upward force from a fluid on an object in it, due to greater pressure at the bottom than the top.
The fluid pushed aside by an object placed in it.
Upthrust on an object equals the weight of fluid it displaces.
When upthrust equals the weight of the object so it rests at the surface.
When the weight of an object is greater than the upthrust on it.
Total mass of an object divided by its total volume, including any hollow spaces.
Single force with the same effect as all the forces acting together.
A liquid or a gas; a substance that can flow.
Cannot easily be squashed into a smaller volume; true of liquids.
Pressure of the air, about 100 kPa, acting on the surface of a liquid.

mistakes.w: Upthrust is caused by the water pushing up.
mistakes.r: Upthrust is caused by the pressure on the bottom of the object being greater than on the top because the bottom is deeper.

mistakes.w: Heavy objects sink and light objects float.
mistakes.r: Objects denser than the liquid sink; objects less dense float (weight compared with upthrust).

mistakes.w: Pressure in a liquid only acts downwards.
mistakes.r: Pressure acts in all directions, at right angles to surfaces.

mistakes.w: A wider container has greater pressure at the bottom.
mistakes.r: Pressure depends only on depth, density and g, not on the shape or width.

mistakes.w: Using depth in cm in p = hρg.
mistakes.r: Convert depth to metres before calculating.

mistakes.w: A floating object has no forces acting on it.
mistakes.r: Weight and upthrust both act; they are equal and opposite, so the resultant is zero.

mistakes.w: Upthrust increases the deeper a fully submerged object goes.
mistakes.r: Once fully submerged, the pressure difference between top and bottom (and so upthrust) stays the same for an incompressible liquid.

mistakes.w: Ships float because steel is light.
mistakes.r: The hull encloses air so the average density of the ship is less than water.

exam.q: State the equation that links pressure due to a column of liquid, height of the column, density of the liquid and gravitational field strength.
model: pressure = height of column × density of liquid × g (p = hρg)
exam.tip: Learn it in words and symbols.

exam.q: Explain why the pressure in a liquid increases with depth.
model: The deeper you go, the more liquid there is above (taller column)
So greater weight of liquid acting on each unit area
exam.tip: Weight of liquid above is the key phrase.

exam.q: Calculate the difference in pressure between the surface and a depth of 4.0 m in water. Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg.
exam.tip: Show the substitution for the first mark.

exam.q: A diver descends from 3 m to 15 m in sea water of density 1030 kg/m³. Calculate the increase in pressure on the diver. g = 10 N/kg.
model: Δp = 123 600 Pa (about 124 kPa)
exam.tip: Use the change in depth, not either depth alone.

exam.q: Explain how a liquid produces an upward force on a submerged object.
model: Pressure increases with depth
The bottom of the object is deeper than the top so pressure on the bottom is greater
Pressure acts at right angles to surfaces so the force upwards on the bottom is greater than the force downwards on the top
The resultant force is upwards: upthrust
exam.tip: Must link depth to pressure difference to force difference.

exam.q: Explain why a block of wood floats on water but a block of iron of the same size sinks.
model: Wood is less dense than water; iron is denser than water
When submerged both displace the same volume so experience the same maximum upthrust
Upthrust can equal the weight of the wood but is less than the weight of the iron
exam.tip: Talk about both density and forces.

exam.q: Explain why a steel ship floats even though steel is denser than water.
model: The hull contains air so the average density of the ship is less than water
It displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight, so upthrust = weight
exam.tip: Use the phrase average density.

exam.q: A boat sails from a river (fresh water) into the sea. Explain what happens to how high it floats.
model: Sea water is denser than fresh water
Less volume needs to be displaced to give an upthrust equal to the weight
So the boat floats higher in the sea
exam.tip: Upthrust stays equal to weight; it is the volume displaced that changes.

exam.q: State two factors that affect the pressure at a point in a liquid.
model: Depth (height of liquid above)
Density of the liquid (also accept gravitational field strength)
exam.tip: Shape of container is not a factor.

exam.q: Describe and explain how the forces from a liquid cause objects to float or sink. Include how pressure varies in a liquid and the factors that decide whether an object floats.
model: Pressure in a liquid is due to the weight of liquid above and increases with depth (p = hρg)
Pressure also increases with density of the liquid
The bottom of an object is deeper so experiences greater pressure and greater upward force than the downward force on top
This gives a resultant upward force, upthrust, equal to the weight of liquid displaced
If upthrust equals weight the object floats; if weight is greater than maximum upthrust it sinks
Object floats if its average density is less than that of the liquid and sinks if greater
Factors: density of object, density of liquid, volume displaced (shape)
exam.tip: Level 3 needs the full chain from pressure to upthrust and a correct float or sink condition.

worked.q: A swimming pool is 2.5 m deep. Calculate the pressure due to the water at the bottom and the total pressure there. Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg, atmospheric pressure = 100 kPa.
steps: p = 25 000 Pa = 25 kPa due to the water
worked.ans: 25 kPa from the water; total pressure 125 kPa

worked.q: A cube of side 0.20 m is fully submerged in water with its top face 0.30 m below the surface. Calculate the upthrust. Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg.
steps: Pressure difference between bottom and top = Δh × ρ × g = 0.20 × 1000 × 10 = 2000 Pa
Check: weight of water displaced = 0.008 m³ × 1000 × 10 = 80 N

worked.q: The cube above has a mass of 5 kg. Does it float or sink? Explain.
steps: Upthrust > weight, so resultant force upwards when held under
It rises until it displaces only 50 N of water: 50 / (1000 × 10) = 0.005 m³
worked.ans: It floats, with 0.005 m³ (five eighths of its volume) below the surface
